subject: Architecture
title: The Iron Bridge: Start of the Industrial Age
description: A 60-second lesson on The Iron Bridge: Start of the Industrial Age.

hook.text: In 1779, the world's first iron bridge opened in England — launching the Industrial Revolution.

buildup.text: Abraham Darby III cast 378 tons of iron to span 100 feet across the River Severn at Coalbrookdale.

discovery.text: The iron pieces were assembled using woodworking joints — mortise and tenon — because bolting iron was new.

twist.text: The bridge proved iron could replace stone and wood in structures — changing construction forever.

climax.text: The town around it renamed itself 'Ironbridge.' The bridge is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

punchline.text: One bridge started the age of metal. The town took its name.

quiz.question: How were the Iron Bridge's pieces joined together?

details.summary: The Iron Bridge at Coalbrookdale, England, completed in 1779, was the world's first major bridge built entirely of cast iron. Its single 30-meter arch used traditional woodworking joints translated into iron, marking the moment when the Industrial Revolution transformed bridge construction forever.
details.whyItMatters: The Iron Bridge symbolizes the transition from traditional to industrial construction. It demonstrated that iron could replace stone and timber for major structures, launching two centuries of metal-based engineering that continues today.
takeaways: World's first major cast-iron bridge, completed in 1779
Its 30-meter arch used woodworking joints translated into iron
It marked the Industrial Revolution's entry into construction

faq.question: Why did they use woodworking joints for an iron bridge?
faq.answer: Nobody had experience designing iron structures at this scale. The builders — including ironmaster Abraham Darby III — applied the joinery techniques they knew from timber construction, using mortise-and-tenon and dovetail joints cast in iron rather than inventing new connection methods.

faq.question: Is the Iron Bridge still standing?
faq.answer: Yes. It's now a pedestrian bridge and UNESCO World Heritage Site. Cast iron's brittleness caused cracking over the centuries, requiring multiple repairs. A major restoration in 2017-2018 repainted it in its original red-brown color after decades in white and gray.
